title: Ghost Dog
intro: Ghost Dog lets its guest voices complicate the opening's confidence that nobody can control you. Jackzebra mocks online outrage as powerless theatre; Chun finds that leaving the city does not escape traps and that money can imprison the person promising to lead others toward it. The final guest makes the stakes concrete: parents, factory work, recruitment deception and threatened confinement. Distrust now has institutions and livelihoods attached. The shift from a violent 'he' to 'we' also prevents the speakers from remaining safely outside the volatility they describe.
reading: Guests revise lead's abstract autonomy with material constraints; distrust acquires family, labour and institutional stakes.

revisions.t46-n1: Jackzebra's claim that nobody can control you is supported by examples of ineffective speech: tantrums, feed flooding and inflated condemnations. The later guest verse introduces a different kind of power, threatening to lock up someone who disobeys. Reading the collaboration as one seamless statement would miss this difference. Some authority is only performance; other authority has a place to put a body. The song contains both experiences.
revisions.t46-phrase-rural-slogan: Chun rejects the easy escape story immediately after invoking it. The rural road has holes, and the same word can mean traps or rip-offs. Changing location therefore does not guarantee a change in the social logic. That matters when a rural newcomer later trusts a crooked intermediary: neither countryside nor city is granted automatic innocence, and moving between them can create new points of vulnerability.
revisions.editorial-46-money-switch: Money traps him, then he tells people who want money to follow him. The speaker occupies both the constrained person and the recruiter promising a way forward. That turn keeps the verse from becoming a simple denunciation of other people's false promises. He recognises the pressure and still speaks its persuasive language. The later wish to slow down further complicates the ambition he advertises.
revisions.t46-n5: The regional word for Dad keeps the family scene intimate. The parents exhaust themselves to send the child out toward a future, and the verse soon places that child amid repetitive factory work and a fraudulent broker. Their care is real even when the route it enables is dangerous. This makes the failure of opportunity hurt at a household scale: the loss includes the hopes and effort invested by people who wanted to help.
revisions.editorial-46-black-broker: The neighbouring factory and rural-newcomer lines make this a labour-placement encounter. The broker's first resource is trust: a young person's need for a route into work makes a claimed connection valuable. The earlier general talk about mixed-interest friendship now has a specific mechanism. An intermediary can present access as assistance while using the applicant's dependence for extraction. The lyric describes that danger without identifying a particular company or case.
revisions.t46-n6: The repeated threat changes the hothead from 'he' to 'we'. That small pronoun change removes the distance that would let the speakers merely inspect other people's brutality. Exploitation has created anger, but the anger also threatens to reproduce harm. When Jackzebra's dismissal of fake tricks returns, it follows a world more materially consequential than the online posturing with which he began.
